The novelty and scale of the dataset are of high value to the community, and the careful design and open release of data and code make it a valuable contribution to the community. Reviewers pointed out some weaknesses in the benchmarking, but I find that these do not detract from the overall value the dataset brings to the community. During the rebuttal the authors addressed reviewer concerns by adding new analyses and clearer baselines. I recommend this paper is accepted.

author_final_remarks.value:
We thank the reviewers for their detailed and thoughtful comments on our manuscript. We were pleased to find that overall the responses to our manuscript were highly positive, with reviewers noting the “high-quality, large-scale” dataset with a “comprehensive evaluation” and a “design that simulates real world variation.” 

The reviewers also offered a range of constructive critiques which, by addressing, we believe has helped improve our manuscript. Notable improvements to our work include:
 - A class-by-class and confusion matrix analysis for unimodal and multimodal models, revealing the contributions of different modalities to multimodal performance
 - A scan of the effects of number of samples included in multisample integration, confirming the k=32 is a solid baseline
 - Inclusion of multiple new imaging models benchmarked, include ViT-L pretrained with CLIP (which is the new high performer for imaging) and the OpenPhenom model, a domain specific imaging model which performs similarly to ImageNet pretrained models.
 - Better descriptions of DeepSet and Set Transformer model architectures
 - A table comparing single modality imaging and gene expression datasets 

We believe that our data and benchmark will help serve the community, and leave fine-tuning and more sophisticated multimodality integration approaches for future work.

We understand the reviewer's concerns regarding addressing points 5 and 6 during the review process.

For 5, we propose including this paragraph in the main text:

    DeepSets and Set Transformers are two examples of permutation invariant and equivariant neural networks designed to operate on sets, where the ordering of elements is inherently arbitrary. DeepSets [Zaheer et al., 2017] introduced a foundational framework for processing such data, showing that any permutation invariant function over a set can be decomposed into a function of summed element-wise transformations: ρ(∑ᵢ φ(xᵢ)). This architecture ensures invariance by construction and has been widely adopted in domains ranging from point cloud processing to graph learning. SetTransformers [Lee et al. 2019] build upon this by incorporating attention mechanisms to capture pairwise and higher-order interactions between elements while maintaining permutation equivariance at the layer level and overall permutation invariance at the output. A subtle but important difference between SetTransformers and vanilla Transformers is the absence of positional encodings, which are unnecessary (and inappropriate) for unordered inputs. Unlike DeepSets, which aggregate early, SetTransformers allow richer inter-element reasoning via self-attention, making them more expressive for tasks where relational structure within sets is important.

We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments, and appreciate their comments about our work being a “rigorous benchmarking framework”, and a “valuable resource for [developing methods] for cellular profiling and drug discovery.” We respond to their remarked limitations below:

1) We agree with the reviewer that more sophisticated multimodal fusion techniques could improve performance on our proposed benchmark. Our goal in this initial release was to establish a clear, interpretable benchmark with reproducible baselines using straightforward fusion strategies. We view scGeneScope as a foundation for future work to explore richer integration methods, and hope it will catalyze further research in that direction. 
2) We agree with the reviewer’s feedback that incorporating a domain-specific vision model for microscopy would be informative. **We now benchmark embeddings extracted by OpenPhenom, a masked autoencoder trained on a large-scale microscopy dataset, on this task, and will incorporate these results into Table 1 of our manuscript.** Interestingly, the OpenPhenom model scores 0.2222 on the Within Experiment benchmark and 0.2511 on the Heldout Experiment benchmark, making it the only Imaging model to score higher on Heldout Experiment than Within Experiment, suggesting that it may be learning more batch invariant features. Even so, its perhaps even more interesting that the OpenPhenom model performs so similarly to the ImageNet Pretrained ViT models, in spite of having such a different training set. We believe that adding these results will improve our manuscript, and appreciate the reviewers suggestions.
3) We agree with the reviewer that our conclusions on our dataset, which focuses on a limited number of chemical compounds, may not fully generalize to real-world drug discovery screens, which generally profile much more chemical compounds than our dataset. We plan to include an explicit acknowledgment of this limitation in our Discussion section. In this dataset, our rationale for focusing on a smaller number of chemical compounds was to improve the reliability and orthogonality of the labels. As the number of chemical compounds grows, it becomes more difficult to ascertain that each of the chemical compounds actually elicits a morphological response from cells. Additionally, the chances that chemical compounds overlap in mechanism of action increases, making treatment identification less aligned with mechanism of action identification. We therefore view the number of chemical compounds as a trade-off between the reliability of labels for benchmarking versus more faithfully simulating the high-throughput nature of drug screening, and we will provide a discussion of this trade-off in our updated manuscript.

We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments, and appreciate that they consider our dataset as “mitigating the lack of multimodal inputs for current treatment-matched tasks”. We respond to their noted limitations below:

1) We agree with the reviewer’s assessment that different replicates will have different kinds of noise associated with them, and that these differences will be amplified when comparing different modalities. In fact, this is the key motivation behind our benchmark, which aims to spur methodological innovation on this challenge, because this property is unavoidable in real-world biological applications involving integrating readouts from multiple destructive modalities. 

    To elaborate, **this design choice reflects realistic experimental constraints and is a common setup in multimodal profiling where destructive assays preclude simultaneous measurements**. In real-world biological applications, researchers necessarily will be comparing samples across different replicates, and need methods that are robust to modality and replicate level noise for this purpose. Second, different modalities have different kinds of technical noise associated with them (e.g. zero drop-out noise in scRNA-seq versus uneven illumination in microscopy), which means latent biological effects of treatments will necessarily be obscured in different ways. Critically, this is not a limitation of our benchmark data, but an inherent limitation of the technologies used to measure cells, and thus these problems will be present in any dataset composed of these modalities (and not just our benchmark). 

    We believe these challenges are not insurmountable for computational methods, and in fact, an entire field of methodology is actively investigating this (“batch effect correction” methods). For example, scVI, which is benchmarked in our paper, is explicitly designed to factorize away replicate-specific noise, to better represent the true biological latent. If these methods are effective at learning noise-invariant embeddings of data, then we expect the success of multimodal integration to increase (and performance using multimodal integration on our benchmark to improve). Hence, our benchmark is likely to spur further methods development on these challenges. 

2) We appreciate the reviewer asking about the effect of the number of samples used. **To address this we performed a sweep over different parameterizations of k, and will report this as a supplementary table.** In general, we find that the effect of increasing k rapidly increases scores between k=2 to k=16 but gains start to taper off by k=32. For instance, on the Within Experiment benchmark, ViT-L-AvgPool goes from 0.3082 accuracy with k=2 up to 0.4416 at k=16, but k=64 does only slightly better than k=32 (0.4823 vs 0.4711 accuracy), and there is no improvement between k=32 and k=64 on the Heldout Experiment benchmark. Overall, we believe that k=32 is a good representation of multisample model performance, but will include the scan of k for models in our Supplementary Material for reference.

3) We thank the reviewer for the suggestion to try different pre-trained models. **In an expansion of our results, we now additionally benchmark image encoders with CLIP weights, as well as the OpenPhenom model, a state-of-the-art public microscopy model trained on large-scale microscopy datasets.** These results will be added to Table 1 in our manuscript. Interestingly, ViT-L trained with CLIP obtains the highest scores on the both Within Experiment and Heldout Experiment benchmarks at 0.2940 and 0.2527 accuracy respectively. Meanwhile, OpenPhenom scores 0.2222 on the Within Experiment benchmark and 0.2511 on the Heldout Experiment benchmark, making it the only Imaging model to score higher on Heldout Experiment than Within Experiment, suggesting that it may be learning more batch invariant features. We believe that adding these results will improve our manuscript, and appreciate the reviewers suggestions.

    Concerning encoder choices, we fixed pretrained weights to ensure reproducibility and isolate performance attributable to the benchmark itself; we agree that encoder fine-tuning is promising, and we plan to explore this in follow-up work. We note that there are many limitations behind fine-tuning that mean that zero-shot evaluation is still highly informative for the community. First, fine-tuning requires substantial compute resources. Second, fine-tuning is not applicable in many single cell analyses, as analyses may be exploratory without clear targets to fine-tune towards (as argued in e.g. work by Kedzierska et al. 2025). Third, foundation models in other domains have shown effective performance in generalizing zero-shot to tasks outside of their training (e.g. protein language models for predicting the impact of synthetic mutations (Notin et al. 2023), or LLMs to time series data (Gruver et al. 2024)). For these reasons, we believe our benchmarks are still informative even if we only report zero-shot performance, as zero-shot performance is a meaningful target that single cell foundation model development should be prioritizing.

4) We agree with the reviewer that a more in-depth analysis of performance on our treatment identification task would be informative. We have completed a supplementary analysis of the class-by-class performance and confusion matrix analysis of the best unimodal models (scVI fit-to-data and ViT-L), as well as their combination in the multimodal single profile model. **One major insight from this analysis is that single cell and imaging models have complementary performance in classifying treatments.** Although scVI performs overall better than ViT-L, there are treatments that imaging can classify strongly but not scRNA-seq (e.g. for Aloxistatin/E-64d, imaging achieves a 77.9% true positive rate (TPR) in Within Experiment and 91% TPR in Heldout Experiment, but scRNA-seq achieves 8.2% TPR in Within Experiment and 6.9% in Heldout Experiment). More importantly, we found cases where multimodal integration yielded higher performance than both unimodal models, with the effect more pronounced in the Heldout Experiment evaluation, indicating stronger generalization. For instance, for PD-98059, scVI achieves 37.2% TPR, ViT only 0.42%, but the multimodal model achieves 66% TPR in Heldout Experiment. Overall, this analysis drives the additional insight that modalities have complementary signal and that multimodal integration can produce synergistic effects between modalities.

5) We appreciate the suggestion and will add a brief introduction to DeepSets and Set Transformers for clarity.

6) We will include a Supplementary table that compares our datasets against existing single modality datasets, focusing on datasets that (like ours) collect single cell read-outs in perturbed contexts. This table will include, for scRNA-seq: L1000 LINCS, SciPlex, Tahoe, and scPerturb; and for microscopy: JUMP CP, RxRx3, BBBC022, BBBC036, and BBBC037. For all datasets, we will list cell line(s), number of treatments, number of cells or samples, measurement technique/readout column, and citation/link to the dataset.

In light of our responses which include scanning the effect of different sample sizes, benchmarking additional models requested by the reviewer, and providing further analysis beyond top-1 accuracy and into the contributions of different modalities, we kindly request that the reviewer consider improving our score into the acceptance range.

One insight from this analysis is that single cell and imaging models have complementary performance in classifying treatments. More importantly, we found cases where multimodal integration yielded higher performance than both unimodal models, with the effect more pronounced in the Heldout Experiment evaluation, indicating stronger generalization. For instance, for PD-98059, scVI achieves 37.2% TPR, ViT only 0.42%, but the multimodal model achieves 66% TPR in the Heldout Experiment. Overall, this analysis drives the additional insight that these modalities have complementary signal and that multimodal integration can produce synergistic effects between modalities. We will include this additional analysis in our Supplemental Material, to strengthen our paper’s contributions and insights.
3) Concatenating the embeddings of greyscale channels when transferring microscopy images to natural image models is a widely established practice that has been previously demonstrated to be superior to other strategies (e.g. Pawlowski et al. 2016, Ando et al. 2017, Hua et al. 2021, Corbe et al. 2023, Xun et al. 2024). To establish that these prior observations also generalize to our data, following the reviewer’s suggestion we performed an additional experiment using averaged embeddings on single profile imaging. As expected from this prior precedent, performance on the Heldout Experiment test split significantly drops when using average image embeddings (16.3%) compared to concatenated embeddings (22%). We will include these additional results in our Supplementary Materials.

summary.value: The paper introduces scGeneScope, a new multimodal dataset and benchmark that pairs single-cell RNA sequencing and Cell Painting microscopy images based on chemical treatments applied to U2-OS cells.  To capture realistic lab variability, the dataset is collected across two distinct experimental rounds. Benchmark evaluations underscore the need for domain-specific datasets in this domain.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Benchmark Design that Simulates Real-World Variation: A major strength is the benchmark's design, which explicitly accounts for experimental variability. The data is split into a Within Experiment test set and a Held-out Experiment test set, where the HE set is derived from a completely independent data generation round. This setup realistically simulates the challenge of applying a model trained on one batch of experiments to new data generated later, exposing models that overfit to technical artifacts versus those that learn robust biological signals.

2. New Community Resource: The paper's primary contribution is the scGeneScope dataset itself. As the authors note, there are no other publicly available resources that couple Cell Painting with scRNA-seq for the same chemical treatments. By releasing a large-scale dataset containing scRNA-seq profiles and single-cell images, the work provides a crucial new resource for developing and testing machine learning methods.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Relatively Simple Multimodal Integration Methods: The multimodal integration methods evaluated are relatively simple.
2. Restricted Evaluation of Foundation Models: The evaluation of foundation models is restricted to a zero-shot setting, which may not reflect their full potential.

strengths_contributions.value:
1, Generation of a high-quality, large-scale matched perturbation transcriptomics and morphology datasets
2. Comprehensive evaluation of the deep learning strategies on the model performance

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper demonstrates that foundation models perform more poorly compared to traditional methods such as scVI. This finding is understandable, as foundation models are primarily trained on in vivo sample datasets rather than in vitro cell line datasets. However, I wonder whether fine-tuning or continual pre-training of the foundation models could lead to performance improvements on this task. This analysis could help us better understand the capabilities of foundation models in this specific application.
2. The authors provide an overall evaluation metric across multiple types of mechanisms of action (MoAs), summarizing the model performance. However, it would also be interesting to investigate the model performance for each individual MoA, such as whether there could be bias toward certain MoAs, and to investigate the underlying reasons. This approach would facilitate a better understanding of the dataset characteristics
3. For the Cell Painting images, which typically contain five imaging channels with each describing a unique molecular feature, the evaluated foundation models utilize traditional image processing approaches, and the authors concatenated embeddings from each channel. Would different feature processing strategies, such as averaging embeddings, lead to different model performance?

This paper proposes a multimodal, treatment-matched dataset including scRNA-seq and Cell Painting microscopy data. The dataset contains a total of 627,704 scRNA-seq gene expression profiles and 716,767 Cell Painting single-cell image crops of U2-OS cells perturbed with 28 chemical treatments. strengths_contributions.value:
1. This dataset mitigates the lack of multimodal inputs for current treatment-matched tasks.

2. The dataset generation process ensures sufficient variability.

3. The description of the dataset and the evaluation protocol is clear.

4. A study of multimodal and multiprofile inputs is conducted.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Since inputs from two different modalities are measured on different replicates, could this introduce noise or perturbation between the two modalities? Moreover, if such noise affects results on multimodal versus single-modality settings (e.g., multimodal inputs might contain more noise), it could challenge the model to effectively extract complementary information from multimodal data.

2. In the multiprofile test setting, a fixed k=32 is chosen; does this choice have a noticeable influence on classification accuracy?

3. Why is a fixed pretrained encoder adopted? Would using a trainable encoder significantly affect performance? Furthermore, ViT and ResNet recently have released different pretrained weights, such as CLIP [1]. Does the paper plan to study the effect of using different pretrained weights?

4. Although the multimodality is a core contribution of this dataset, the paper only studies combinations of modalities in terms of classification accuracy. It is recommended to conduct further analysis on the contribution of each modality and the model's preference for different modalities.

5. It is recommended to include a brief introduction of the adopted aggregation methods, such as DeepSets and Set Transformers.

6. It would be helpful to show a comparative table with existing single-modality datasets.

summary.value: This manuscript introduces scGeneScope, a conditionally paired multimodal dataset combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and Cell Painting microscopy images in response to chemical treatments. Designed to advance machine learning methods for cellular profiling, the dataset includes 28 chemicals targeting distinct biological pathways, applied to U2-OS cells across two experimental rounds. Each modality was independently profiled, enabling realistic evaluation of unimodal, multimodal, and multiprofile models under experimental variability. Benchmarking reveals that multiprofile integration enhances model performance, particularly in unimodal settings, and that traditional fit-to-data models outperform recent scRNA-seq foundation models in zero-shot mode. The dataset and code are publicly released to facilitate further research and rigorous benchmarking in biological machine learning.

strengths_contributions.value:
- This manuscript presents scGeneScope, a large-scale, well-controlled dataset comprising 627,704 scRNA-seq profiles and 716,767 Cell Painting images of U2-OS cells treated with 28 diverse chemical compounds. The scGeneScope is generated through paired replicate experiments conducted under tightly controlled and documented variability, enabling robust comparisons and integration of transcriptomic and imaging modalities.
- The manuscript defines a rigorous benchmarking framework to evaluate model performance in identifying mechanisms of action (MoAs), incorporating both Within Experiment and Held-out Experiment splits. This design allows assessment of model generalization under realistic laboratory conditions and experimental variability.
- The scGeneScope dataset and benchmarking code are publicly released, providing a valuable resource for developing, testing, and benchmarking unimodal, multimodal, and multiprofile machine learning models for cellular profiling and drug discovery.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- While Section 5.2 investigates a simple late-stage conditional fusion strategy for integrating scRNA-seq and imaging modalities, the manuscript does not explore more advanced multimodal fusion techniques, such as cross-modal relationship modeling or cross-attention-based integration methods. These approaches have shown promise in capturing richer inter-modal interactions and could potentially enhance treatment classification performance. The absence of such evaluations limits the study’s insight into the full potential of multimodal learning strategies.
- The imaging models evaluated in this study are all pretrained on natural image datasets (e.g., ImageNet). While convenient, this approach may restrict the models’ ability to effectively capture biologically relevant features in Cell Painting images, which differ significantly from natural scenes. The manuscript would benefit from considering or benchmarking against domain-specific models trained on microscopy data or incorporating classical feature extraction baselines such as CellProfiler.
- Although the dataset includes 28 chemical compounds spanning diverse mechanisms of action (MoAs), this coverage remains narrow relative to the complexity and scale of real-world drug discovery, which often involves profiling hundreds to thousands of perturbations across multiple doses and cell lines. The manuscript should acknowledge this limitation and discuss the implications for generalizability and scalability of the benchmark in practical applications.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The added experiments with OpenPhenom, the clarified rationale for methodological choices, and the explicit acknowledgment of dataset limitations strengthen the manuscript. I will maintain my score leading toward acceptance.

title.value: scGeneScope: A Treatment-Matched Single Cell Imaging and Transcriptomics Dataset and Benchmark for Treatment Response Modeling

TLDR.value: We create a perturbationally-paired single cell imaging and transcriptomics dataset and benchmark and evaluate unimodal, multimodal, and multisample imaging and scRNA-seq models for treatment response modeling; HF data access token in zip.

abstract.value: Understanding cellular responses to chemical interventions is critical to the discovery of effective therapeutics. Because individual biological techniques often measure only one axis of cellular response at a time, high-quality multimodal datasets are needed to unlock a holistic understanding of how cells respond to treatments and to advance computational methods that integrate modalities. However, many techniques destroy cells and thus preclude paired measurements, and attempts to match disparate unimodal datasets are often confounded by data being generated in incompatible experimental settings. Here we introduce scGeneScope, a multimodal single‑cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and Cell Painting microscopy image dataset conditionally paired by chemical treatment, designed to facilitate the development and benchmarking of unimodal, multimodal, and multiple profile machine learning methods for cellular profiling. 28 chemicals, each acting on distinct biological pathways or mechanisms of action (MoAs), were applied to U2-OS cells in two experimental data generation rounds, creating paired sets of replicates that were then profiled independently by scRNA‑seq or Cell Painting. Using scGeneScope, we derive a replicate- and experiment-split treatment identification benchmark simulating MoA discovery under realistic laboratory variability conditions and evaluate unimodal, multimodal, and multiprofile models ranging in complexity from linear approaches to recent foundation models. Multiprofile integration improved performance in both the unimodal and multimodal settings, with gains more consistent in the former. Evaluation of unimodal models for MoA identification demonstrated that recent scRNA-seq foundation models deployed zero-shot were consistently outperformed by classic fit-to-data methods, underscoring the need for careful, realistic benchmarking in machine learning for biology. We release the scGeneScope dataset and benchmarking code to support further research.
